ethiopia.title: ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English
ethiopia.content: ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer October 25, 2026 (ENA) The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), marking 119 years of institutional development, represents a longstanding pillar of Ethiopia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national security. From defending the country’s independence to participating in international peacekeeping operations and expanding domestic defense manufacturing, the institution has continued to evolve in response to changing national, regional and global security demands. Today, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation that extends beyond conventional military strength. Reforms in organizational structure, professional training, technological development and defense production are intended to strengthen its operational capabilities and reduce dependence on external suppliers. At the same time, its contributions to peace and security at national, regional and international levels remain important dimensions of its institutional responsibilities. The development of the force reflects the relationship between national defense, institutional resilience and technological capacity. Its future effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment it possesses, but also on the professionalism of its personnel, the strength of its institutions and its ability to contribute to lasting peace. Resilience Legacy Ethiopia’s military history is closely connected with its struggle to preserve independence and territorial integrity. Across successive generations, the country’s armed forces have defended national sovereignty while adapting to changing political circumstances, military doctrines and technological developments. The ENDF’s historical legacy includes the wider tradition of Ethiopian resistance to colonial aggression, notably the victory at Adwa in 1896, as well as the military experiences that shaped the country’s subsequent defense institutions. These historical milestones preceded the establishment of the modern army and helped shape the national consciousness surrounding sovereignty and independence. Over the decades, the armed forces have undergone changes in command structures, training systems, equipment and operational responsibilities. The contemporary ENDF is building on this historical experience while seeking to develop a more professional, technologically capable and institutionally resilient force. The reform agenda pursued in recent years places particular emphasis on organizational unity, operational readiness, specialized capabilities and modern military science. In July 2026, ENDF Chief of Staff Field Marshal Birhanu Jula said the force had strengthened its unity, expanded its organizational structure and continued modernizing its equipment and technology amid an increasingly complex security environment. These efforts, he said, were intended to reinforce its capacity to safeguard Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The significance of this transformation lies in its effort to connect historical experience with the requirements of contemporary national defense. A modern military must combine discipline and institutional continuity with scientific knowledge, technical expertise and the capacity to respond to rapidly changing security conditions. A Pillar of National Peace The ENDF’s principal constitutional responsibility is to defend Ethiopia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Its contribution to national peace also involves protecting the country against armed threats, responding to security emergencies and supporting conditions in which citizens can pursue their social and economic activities in safety. National peace, however, extends beyond military operations. Sustainable stability requires functioning institutions, political dialogue, reconciliation, respect for the law and public confidence. The defense force can contribute to these objectives by maintaining professionalism, observing constitutional responsibilities and protecting civilians in accordance with applicable law. The ENDF’s experience in complex security environments has reinforced the importance of coordination, intelligence, training and operational preparedness. Its ongoing institutional reforms seek to strengthen these capabilities while adapting to emerging threats. The force’s relationship with the public is equally important. National defense is most effective when the military operates as a professional institution serving the country and its people, rather than a particular political interest. Maintaining political neutrality, respecting civilian authority and upholding the rights of citizens are essential to sustaining public trust. The military’s role in national peace should therefore be assessed not only through its ability to confront armed threats, but also through its adherence to the law, protection of civilians and contribution to an environment conducive to reconciliation and development. In a country with diverse communities and complex social and political dynamics, lasting peace requires cooperation among security institutions, public authorities, communities and other stakeholders. The ENDF’s professional conduct and institutional accountability are important to this broader national effort. Regional Security Ethiopia occupies a strategically important position in the Horn of Africa, a region where security developments frequently cross-national borders. The ENDF’s contribution to regional peace includes cooperation with neighboring countries and participation in regional security mechanisms. Ethiopia has maintained an important role in the Eastern Africa Standby Force, an African regional arrangement designed to support peace operations and respond to crises. In May 2026, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula reaffirmed Ethiopia’s commitment to regional peace and security during discussions with the outgoing and incoming leadership of the Eastern Africa Standby Force. The meeting highlighted the importance of regional cooperation in addressing shared security challenges. Such cooperation demonstrates that national defense and regional stability are interconnected. Information sharing, military coordination, joint preparedness and professional exchanges can help countries respond more effectively to threats that no single state can address independently. The ENDF’s regional responsibilities must also be understood within the broader principle that durable security cannot be achieved through military measures alone. Diplomatic engagement, peaceful settlement of disputes, economic cooperation and respect for national sovereignty remain essential to preventing conflicts and strengthening relations among neighboring countries. A stable Horn of Africa would create greater opportunities for regional trade, infrastructure development, investment and economic integration. By contributing to legitimate regional security arrangements and supporting cooperative approaches to shared threats, Ethiopia’s defense institutions can help create conditions for these wider development objectives. International Peacekeeping One of the most visible expressions of Ethiopia’s contribution to international peace has been its participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. Ethiopian personnel have served in international missions for decades, reflecting the country’s longstanding engagement with multilateral efforts to maintain peace and protect communities affected by conflict. According to the United Nations, Ethiopia’s participation in UN-authorized operations dates back to 1951, when Ethiopian personnel served as part of the multinational force in the Korean War. Since then, Ethiopian military personnel have contributed to peace and security operations in different parts of the world. A prominent example is the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA), established in 2011 to help stabilize the disputed Abyei area between Sudan and South Sudan. The mission monitors security arrangements, supports the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and contributes to efforts to prevent renewed violence. The deployment of Ethiopian troops to Abyei followed an agreement reached by Sudanese and South Sudanese representatives in Addis Ababa. The mission illustrates how Ethiopian military personnel have supported internationally mandated security arrangements in a sensitive border region. Ethiopian personnel have also served in other United Nations missions, including operations in South Sudan. Their responsibilities have included supporting civilian protection, maintaining security in designated areas and helping create conditions for humanitarian activities and political processes. These experiences have given Ethiopian peacekeepers opportunities to work within multinational command structures, cooperate with personnel from different countries and apply international peacekeeping standards in demanding operational environments. International peacekeeping also strengthens professional experience. Service in multinational missions exposes military personnel to different approaches to logistics, communication, civilian protection and operational coordination. Lessons gained from these assignments can contribute to training and institutional development at home. The broader significance of Ethiopia’s peacekeeping record is that military capability can serve purposes beyond national defense. When deployed under an authorized mandate and in accordance with international law, disciplined military personnel can help protect vulnerable populations, support humanitarian access and contribute to efforts to restore stability. Defense Technology, Industrial Capacity Alongside its peace and security responsibilities, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation in military technology and domestic production. The objective is to strengthen the country’s ability to manufacture, maintain and sustain essential defense equipment while developing the technical expertise required for modern military operations. For a country with extensive security responsibilities, dependence on foreign suppliers can affect the availability, maintenance and long-term sustainability of military equipment. Developing domestic production capacity can help reduce these vulnerabilities, retain technical knowledge and build a stronger industrial foundation for national defense. Ethiopia’s defense industrial institutions provide important examples of this approach. The Homicho Ammunition Engineering Complex is associated with domestic ammunition production, while the wider defense industry has been working to strengthen capabilities in equipment manufacturing, engineering and maintenance. These facilities illustrate how defense production can bring together mechanical engineering, industrial processes, technical training and specialized manufacturing. Their strategic importance lies not simply in the products they manufacture, but also in the knowledge and skills developed through sustained industrial activity. Developing domestic expertise in this field can also expand opportunities for engineering research and technical education. Another significant step came in June 2026, when the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Air Force signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a drone technology center and strengthen research, laboratory cooperation and aerospace capabilities. The initiative is intended to support innovation and the development of local expertise in unmanned aerial systems. In August 2026, the ENDF and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute also signed a cooperation agreement to explore the application of artificial intelligence in areas including logistics, military training, cybersecurity, military healthcare, air operations and electronic warfare. The agreement points to a broader shift in defense modernization. Military effectiveness increasingly depends on the ability to collect, process and use information, maintain secure communications and support rapid, informed decision-making. Artificial intelligence and related digital technologies could contribute to these objectives, although their operational benefits will depend on research, testing, qualified personnel and effective implementation. These initiatives demonstrate that Ethiopia’s defense transformation is not limited to acquiring modern equipment. It also involves building the scientific, industrial and educational capabilities required to develop and sustain advanced systems. Human Capital Dimension Technology alone cannot create an effective defense institution. Modern military systems require skilled operators, engineers, technicians, researchers, maintenance specialists and commanders capable of applying scientific knowledge to operational requirements. For this reason, investment in military education and professional development is central to the ENDF’s modernization. Military academies, specialized training institutions and cooperation with civilian research organizations can help develop the expertise needed to operate sophisticated equipment and maintain complex systems. The partnership between the ENDF, the Ethiopian Air Force, the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute illustrates the potential value of cooperation between defense institutions and the wider scientific community. Such partnerships can strengthen research capacity, encourage the exchange of technical knowledge and support the development of locally relevant solutions. They can also help cultivate a generation of Ethiopian engineers and researchers whose expertise may contribute to defense manufacturing and other technology-intensive sectors. Domestic defense production can generate benefits beyond the military when it develops transferable industrial skills, strengthens engineering capacity and encourages research and innovation. The long-term objective is to build a system in which training, research, manufacturing and operational requirements reinforce one another. This would enable Ethiopia to develop more of the expertise necessary to maintain its defense capabilities while creating a stronger foundation for technological advancement. Self-Reliance The ENDF’s industrial and technological transformation forms part of Ethiopia’s wider pursuit of productive capacity and economic self-reliance. Similar priorities are evident in the country’s efforts to expand agricultural production, develop mineral resources, strengthen manufacturing and invest in scientific knowledge. Defense production has a distinct purpose because it is directly connected to national security. Nevertheless, it can contribute to broader industrial development by encouraging specialized engineering, technical training and domestic manufacturing. The development of ammunition production, engineering facilities and drone research demonstrates the range of capabilities required to build a more self-reliant defense sector. These initiatives can help strengthen maintenance capacity, improve the availability of selected equipment and create opportunities for domestic technical expertise. It is important, however, to distinguish progress in selected areas from complete self-sufficiency. Modern military systems depend on extensive supply chains involving specialized components, software, materials and technical knowledge. Building sustainable domestic capacity is therefore a continuing process that requires investment, research, reliable production standards and international technical cooperation where necessary. The strongest measure of progress is not the number of factories established or the equipment acquired, but the ability to produce reliable systems, maintain them over time, develop skilled personnel and meet clearly identified national defense requirements. A more capable domestic defense industry can strengthen strategic autonomy by giving Ethiopia greater control over parts of its supply chains. It can also improve the country’s capacity to respond to changing security requirements without relying exclusively on external procurement. The Road Ahead As the ENDF marks 119 years of institutional development, its future will be shaped by its ability to combine historical experience with professional standards, technological innovation and a commitment to peace. Its responsibilities remain broad: protecting national sovereignty, contributing to domestic security within the law, supporting regional stability and participating in international peacekeeping. Meeting these responsibilities requires an institution that is well trained, technically capable, disciplined and accountable. The development of domestic defense industries, drone technology and artificial intelligence cooperation indicates a growing emphasis on technological preparedness. Sustaining these efforts will require stronger research institutions, skilled human resources, effective industrial management and continued adaptation to changing military technologies. Equally important is the relationship between security and peace. Military readiness can deter threats and help protect communities, but lasting stability also depends on dialogue, diplomacy, reconciliation and cooperation among nations and communities. The ENDF’s long-term contribution will be strengthened when professional defense capabilities complement these wider efforts. The force’s 119-year institutional journey thus represents both a historical legacy and a continuing responsibility. Its achievements in national defense, regional cooperation, international peacekeeping and technological development provide a foundation on which further progress can be built. Ultimately, the strength of the Ethiopian National Defense Force will be measured not only by its capacity to defend the country, but also by its professionalism, its contribution to a secure regional environment and its ability to adapt responsibly to the demands of modern defense. By combining institutional resilience with technological advancement and a sustained commitment to peace, the ENDF can continue to serve as an important pillar of Ethiopia’s sovereignty and national development. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) recently celebrated its 119th anniversary, highlighting its crucial role in safeguarding Ethiopia's sovereignty and contributing to regional stability. The ENDF has evolved significantly, focusing on reforms in organizational structure, professional training, and technological advancements to enhance its operational capabilities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. Its historical legacy, rooted in the defense of national independence, informs its current transformation towards a more professional and technologically adept military. The ENDF's responsibilities extend beyond military operations to include promoting national peace through civilian protection and institutional accountability. Additionally, the force plays a vital role in regional security cooperation and international peacekeeping, participating in UN missions since 1951. Recent initiatives aim to bolster Ethiopia's defense technology and domestic production capabilities, exemplified by the establishment of a drone technology center. These efforts are designed to ensure sustainable national defense while fostering regional cooperation and economic development.

Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Fighting erupts near Baidoa as Somali army advance on Burhakabo stalls Fighting erupts near Baidoa as Somali army advance on Burhakabo stalls October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted on Monday on the outskirts of Baidoa between the Somali National Army and forces loyal to Abdiaziz Laftagareen, the former president of Southwest State. An official from Laftagareen’s faction said army units had been ambushed on the road. The soldiers were travelling through the Burjed area, near Baidoa, reportedly on their way to Burhakabo. The town lies 60km east of Baidoa and was recently seized from the federal government by Laftagareen’s forces. The official said their fighters attacked because the soldiers wanted to pose for photographs on the edge of Baidoa and then claim to have carried out an operation. Laftagareen’s group said it killed dozens of soldiers and destroyed a number of military vehicles. Neither figure has been independently confirmed. The federal government and its ally, the current Southwest State administration, have not yet responded. The clashes come as militant attacks continue to stall about 2,000 Somali troops who set out on Saturday from Baledogle airfield, on the Mogadishu-Baidoa road, to retake Burhakabo and other towns in the Bay region that Laftagareen’s forces recently captured. The troops, travelling with more than 200 military vehicles, are now stranded in Leego, about 50km east of Burhakabo and close to Baledogle airfield. Reports indicate that the militant group Al-Shabaab has mined the entire road. On Saturday, local media reported that Al-Shabaab ambushed the convoy, sparking hours of fighting that caused casualties on both sides. The army said it gained the upper hand and killed seven militants. Al-Shabaab-affiliated media reported that 10 soldiers were killed and four military vehicles destroyed. Local media say the advance has stalled mainly because of fears of landmines and further ambushes. Residents said security forces ordered them to leave Leego, warning that the town could be hit by Turkish air strikes. Leego is currently held by the Somali military, with militants positioned on its outskirts. The federal government is seeking to consolidate its control of Southwest State, where it installed a loyal administration led by former parliament speaker Adan Madobe. It ousted regional President Abdiasis Mohamed Hassan Laftagareen in March in a military offensive backed by Turkish air power. Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 26-10-2026, 12:13PM MOGADISHU — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud whose presidential term expired in May 2026 travelled to Uganda hours after inviting opposition groups and the leaders of the semi-autonomous states of Puntland and Jubaland to talks next month aimed at addressing a deepening dispute over federal elections. The timing of the trip comes as political and constitutional tensions intensify in Somalia, particularly over the president’s term in office and the country’s electoral system. During a meeting in Entebbe in August 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni reportedly pressed Hassan Sheikh to engage with Somali opposition groups and seek a negotiated settlement to the country’s growing political crisis. Museveni was also reported to have warned that Uganda could withdraw its troops from Somalia if the government failed to reach an agreement with political stakeholders opposed to its proposed electoral system. The opposition has accused the administration of pursuing an electoral framework that has deepened political divisions and created uncertainty over the country’s democratic transition. Uganda is a major troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which supports Somali security forces in their fight against Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. Kampala is concerned that a prolonged political deadlock in Mogadishu could distract the government and security institutions from counterinsurgency operations and undermine the stability of the African Union mission. Although the Somali presidency has not publicly confirmed that the latest trip is directly linked to the election dispute or Uganda’s reported concerns, its timing has drawn attention to Kampala’s potential role in efforts to ease the political crisis. Museveni has reportedly urged Somali leaders to engage in inclusive dialogue, stressing the need for a political settlement that would allow the country to maintain its security gains and strengthen state institutions. Uganda has also emphasised the importance of building a capable Somali national army that can eventually assume full responsibility for the country’s security as African Union forces withdraw. The transition is part of broader plans to transfer security duties to Somali forces by 2027. Museveni has expressed concern that Ugandan troops could face continued risks while Somali political leaders remain divided over the distribution of power and the electoral process. Uganda has played a central role in international security efforts in Somalia for years, with its troops forming a key part of the African Union’s military presence. The political dispute therefore carries implications beyond the electoral process, potentially affecting the fight against Al-Shabaab and plans to transfer security responsibilities to Somali forces. Hassan Sheikh’s invitation to opposition leaders and the subsequent trip to Uganda come at a sensitive moment for Somalia, as efforts to reach an agreement over elections face competing political demands and uncertainty over the country’s constitutional future. somalia.summary: The climate crisis is severely impacting Somalia, leading to widespread hunger among its population. Currently, approximately 5.4 million people in the country are facing food insecurity, primarily due to prolonged drought conditions that have devastated livestock, which many Somalis rely on for their livelihoods. Mohamed Abdi, the Somalia country director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, emphasizes the dire situation, highlighting that the ongoing climate challenges are exacerbating existing vulnerabilities. The combination of climate change and its effects on agriculture and livestock is creating a humanitarian crisis, necessitating urgent international attention and assistance. As the situation worsens, the need for sustainable solutions to address both immediate food needs and long-term climate resilience becomes increasingly critical for the affected communities in Somalia.

Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023. Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images Global development US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy? Supported by About this content Mark Townsend in Kismayo Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia , never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river. “The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.” View image in fullscreen Cayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba. “The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.” Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab , the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets. The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa , in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians. The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital . Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño , forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month. View image in fullscreen An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia. Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead. “The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source. When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people . Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm. Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies , said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.” View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country. Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.” Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño . L ike many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.” Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023 : her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater. “In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old. US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) , meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”. View image in fullscreen Arbey Abdi Famu, a resident of the Dalhiska displacement camp in Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000. Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland , is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half. His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba. View image in fullscreen People on the streets of Kismayo, where long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says. The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled. Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient. “They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks. C orroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”. Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets. Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said. Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.” Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter. “ It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.” Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided. View image in fullscreen A mother takes her baby to a Somalia Red Crescent Society health centre in Kismayo to check for symptoms of malnutrition. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes. Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region. Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year. David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.” View image in fullscreen A malnourished three-month-old baby in Kismayo hospital’s intensive-care ward in September. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.” Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia. Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger . Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them. Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart. Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.” In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea. El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine. Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year. Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night. View image in fullscreen Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness. “She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived. Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse. somalia.summary: US forces in Somalia are facing accusations of "weaponising" the country's floods amid a military campaign against the Islamist group al-Shabaab. Reports indicate that coordinated airstrikes are forcing civilians to seek refuge near the flood-prone River Juba, exacerbating their vulnerability as El Niño intensifies the rainy season. Eyewitness accounts describe a relentless barrage of airstrikes, leading to significant civilian casualties and destruction in towns like Jilib. Critics argue that the US military strategy appears to exploit the flooding to weaken al-Shabaab, raising ethical concerns about the use of humanitarian data for military purposes. While US officials deny targeting civilians or using weather as a weapon, the situation remains dire, with insufficient flood defenses and a lack of humanitarian aid. The International Committee of the Red Cross warns of severe flooding, and local authorities express concern over the potential for large-scale displacement and loss of life as conditions worsen.

As the political and security landscape in the wider Red Sea region evolves, three separatist projects have emerged as pivotal: In Sudan, the 'Tasis' coalition, supported by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia and their political allies, formed an alternative government in Nyala, South Darfur, in July 2025. They began establishing their own quasi-state administration in the Darfur and Kordofan regions, effectively partitioning Sudan. In December 2025, Israel officially recognised Somaliland as an independent state, with its capital in Hargeisa. Somaliland’s authorities accelerated their outreach to the US government in an attempt to win recognition from Donald Trump’s administration. This hindered the progress of Somali-Somaliland negotiations on the future of the territory. Also in December 2025, the Yemeni separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) took control of almost the entire territory of the former People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. In January 2026, the STC published a draft constitution for the projected State of South Arabia. However, efforts to restore independence to Yemen's southern provinces were swiftly suppressed by the central government, the Presidential Leadership Council, and Saudi Arabia. The security vacuum that resulted encouraged the Houthis to escalate. This regional wave of separatisms resulted from a combination of internal dynamics within individual states and the projection of influence by regional actors, particularly the UAE and Israel. These countries have sought to drastically reshape the regional security status quo and expand their influence. While there is no universal model of secession, the movements and their regional backers in each of the three cases seek to normalise unilateral changes to borders, adding a new strain on international law and multilateralism. For this reason, these processes remain highly relevant to the EU. Throughout this seminar, participants will discuss the internal and external factors that determine the rise and decline of separatist movements in the region, addressing the following questions: What is the current strength of separatist movements and secessionist governments in the region? What role do regional parties' foreign patrons and sponsors, such as the UAE, Israel or Saudi Arabia, play in accelerating or thwarting these projects? How do other actors, such as neighbouring states, international organisations and foreign stakeholders, approach this issue? What position should the EU and the US take regarding last year's developments around the Red Sea? Agenda: 12:00-12:30 Arrivals. Sandwich lunch. 12:30-12:35 Welcome and opening remarks Melchior Szczepanik, Head of Brussels Office, PISM 12:35-13:30 Panel Discussion Jędrzej Czerep, Head of the Middle East and Africa Programme, Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM) Mihai Sebastian Chihaia, Policy Analyst, European Policy Centre Rossella Marangio, Senior Analyst, EU Institute for Strategic Studies (online) Julia Sochacka, Middle East Analyst, PISM Maike Tribbels, Head of Division, Horn of Africa, East Africa, European External Action Service Moderator: Melchior Szczepanik, Head of Brussels Office, PISM 13:30-14:00 Exchange of views with participants The debate will be held under the Chatham House Rule. somalia.summary: The Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM) is hosting a roundtable discussion on November 6, 2026, focusing on separatist movements in Somalia, Yemen, and Sudan, as well as the geopolitical dynamics in the Red Sea region. This event coincides with the release of a PISM report titled “New Flags in the Red Sea Region,” which analyzes the rise of separatist projects. Key developments include the formation of a quasi-state in Sudan by the 'Tasis' coalition, Somaliland's push for international recognition following Israel's acknowledgment, and the Southern Transitional Council's control over former Yemeni territories. These movements are influenced by internal state dynamics and external support from regional powers like the UAE and Israel, which aim to reshape the regional security landscape. The discussion will explore the implications of these separatist movements for international law and the responses of the EU and the US to these developments. Participants will engage in a debate under the Chatham House Rule.

somalia.content: Mogadishu Discharges Citizen Linked to Kenyan Ebola Victim After 21-Day Monitoring - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Health Nationwide Mogadishu Discharges Citizen Linked to Kenyan Ebola Victim After 21-Day Monitoring October 26, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Ministry of Health and Human Services has released a Somali citizen from quarantine after two separate tests confirmed he was not infected with the Ebola virus, following his direct contact with an Ebola patient who died in Kenya on October 5, 2026. According to a press release issued by the Ministry on October 24 , the citizen was placed in quarantine on October 12 at the Ebola quarantine and treatment centre at Forlanini Hospital in Mogadishu. The Ministry said the man had been in direct contact with a person who died of Ebola in Kenya, and that he was quarantined safely and with dignity in accordance with international health procedures. The Ministry conducted two tests during the quarantine period. The first test, carried out in Somalia on October 12, returned negative. On October 19, the Ministry sent a second sample to a laboratory abroad to confirm the result. That test also came back negative on October 23, definitively confirming that the man was not infected with the virus. The Ministry said the citizen showed no symptoms of Ebola during quarantine and had completed the 21-day health monitoring period counted from October 3, the last day he had contact with the infected person. Based on the two test results, the completion of the monitoring period, the man’s health status, and a public health risk assessment, the Ministry decided to release him from quarantine in line with national and international health guidelines. No Confirmed Case in Somalia The Ministry reiterated that no Ebola case has been confirmed in Somalia to date, and that the quarantined man was a case that had originated outside the country. It said it would continue to strengthen disease surveillance, preparedness at points of entry, and measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases. The Ministry urged the public to obtain health information from official sources and to avoid spreading unverified reports. It also provided a list of Ebola symptoms, including sudden fever, severe fatigue, muscle pain, headache, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, and unexplained bleeding, and advised anyone experiencing these symptoms to contact the toll-free number 995. The Initial Quarantine and Tracing Operation The case began when Somalia’s International Health Regulations office received an official notification from Uganda on the evening of October 10, stating that a Somali citizen and a Kenyan citizen had travelled together from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the initial quarantine , the two men stayed in the same hotel and took the same taxi to Entebbe Airport before separating. The Somali citizen flew to Mogadishu via Addis Ababa, while the Kenyan citizen travelled to Nairobi, where he later died of Ebola. The Ugandan report included the Somali citizen’s name, passport number, flight details and seat number. A joint investigation lasting nearly 24 hours, involving the Immigration Agency, the Criminal Investigation Department, the Ministry of Health, and the National Institute of Health, succeeded in safely quarantining the citizen at Forlanini Hospital. The Ministry also quarantined ten other Somali citizens who had returned from the DRC through Uganda, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the expanded quarantine measures . Those individuals were also undergoing laboratory testing and medical monitoring. The Regional Context The release comes as Kenya continues to manage its own Ebola cluster. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Kenya’s outbreak , all 135 contacts linked to the index case in Kenya have been traced, and the first group of quarantined contacts has begun returning home. The Kenyan index patient transited through Uganda and flew to Nairobi without being detected at the airport. A similar case arriving in Mogadishu would encounter screening systems that a WHO assessment rated at 20 percent capacity, with no dedicated isolation areas and no biosecure transport. Somalia has taken steps to strengthen its preparedness. In May, the government convened a high-level national conference on Ebola readiness at the National Public Health Emergency Operations Center, bringing together security, foreign affairs, health, civil aviation, and disaster management officials, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the national preparedness meeting . In October, following Kenya’s first case, the Cabinet approved the establishment of a national Ebola preparedness committee composed of six ministries and chaired by the Second Deputy Prime Minister, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Cabinet decision . However, the Cabinet’s own assessment noted that Somalia’s points of entry have International Health Regulations core capacities of only 20 percent, and the federal government does not control all airports and borders. Critical Note The release of the quarantined citizen is a welcome development, and the Ministry of Health deserves credit for the transparent and methodical way it handled the case. The decision to send a second sample to an international laboratory, rather than relying solely on the domestic test, reflects a commendable commitment to accuracy. The public communication was clear, the timeline was documented, and the release was based on a combination of laboratory results, clinical observation, and risk assessment. But the case also illustrates the fragility of Somalia’s position. The citizen was quarantined because he had contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya. That patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda and arrived in Nairobi without being detected. Somalia’s ability to detect a similar case at its own points of entry remains limited, as the WHO assessment of 20 percent capacity demonstrates. The Ministry’s statement that no Ebola case has been confirmed in Somalia is accurate, but it is not a guarantee for the future. The DRC outbreak continues to accelerate, with more than 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,500 deaths. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or specific treatment. Kenya’s cluster appears contained, but the movement of people across East Africa is constant. The quarantined man was released because he was not infected. The next case may not be so fortunate. الأربعاء المقبل الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا 26 أكتوبر 2026 12:00 ص وكالات - واصل الأفريقي التونسي مشواره في دوري أبطال أفريقيا لكرة القدم، بعدما حجز بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات بفوزه على ضيفه تي بي مازيمبي، بطل الكونغو الديمقراطية، بهدف دون رد، الأحد، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني للمسابقة. وسجل الكاميروني تاديوس نكينغ هدف المباراة الوحيد في الدقيقة الثانية من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط الأول، ليمنح الفريق التونسي انتصاراً ثميناً على أرضه، بعد مواجهة اتسمت بأهمية كبيرة للطرفين. وكانت مباراة الذهاب، التي أُقيمت في مدينة لومومباشي الكونغولية الأسبوع الماضي، قد انتهت بالتعادل 1-1، ليحسم الأفريقي التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 2-1. وبهذا الإنجاز، أصبح الأفريقي الممثل الثاني للكرة التونسية في مرحلة المجموعات هذا الموسم، إلى جانب غريمه التقليدي الترجي التونسي، فيما تبخرت آمال مازيمبي في مواصلة مشواره نحو اللقب السادس في تاريخه، والأول منذ عام 2015. ويطمح الأفريقي إلى استعادة أمجاده القارية والمنافسة على لقبه الثاني في البطولة، بعدما سبق له التتويج بدوري أبطال أفريقيا عام 1991. نواذيبو الموريتاني يقلب تأخره ويعبر إلى المرحلة الرئيسية وفي العاصمة الموريتانية نواكشوط، انتزع نواذيبو بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما تغلب على ضيفه سان بيدرو الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-0، على ملعب «شيخ ولد بيديا»، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وبدأ الفريق الموريتاني المواجهة بقوة، وافتتح كارتييه ديمبيلي التسجيل في الدقيقة العاشرة، ليمنح أصحاب الأرض تقدماً مبكراً أعاد المواجهة إلى نقطة التعادل في مجموع المباراتين. وفي الدقيقة 53، أضاف شيخ خطاب الهدف الثاني لنواذيبو، ليعزز فرص فريقه في حسم بطاقة التأهل ويمنحه الأفضلية اللازمة بعد خسارة مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 2-1 خارج أرضه. وبهذا الفوز، عوض نواذيبو خسارته في اللقاء الأول، ليتفوق بنتيجة 3-2 في مجموع المباراتين، ويواصل حضوره في المنافسات القارية، بعدما نجح في استثمار عاملي الأرض والجمهور لحسم المواجهة. ويمثل التأهل خطوة مهمة للنادي الموريتاني، الذي نجح في تجاوز عقبة منافس إيفواري بعد مواجهة امتدت حساباتها إلى المباراتين، ليحجز مكانه بين أندية مرحلة المجموعات. المغرب الفاسي يحسم التأهل بهدف قاتل في أبيدجان بدوره، تأهل المغرب الفاسي إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما حقق فوزاً ثميناً على أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-1 في العاصمة أبيدجان، مستفيداً من تعادله في مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 1-1 في مكناس. وبعد انتهاء الشوط الأول بالتعادل السلبي، افتتح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي التسجيل للمغرب الفاسي، قبل أن يتمكن كيفين باكارا من إدراك التعادل لأسيك ميموزا، لتزداد صعوبة المواجهة مع اقتراب نهايتها. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه إلى ركلات الترجيح، خطف خالد بابا هدف الفوز للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع، ليمنح فريقه انتصاراً خارج أرضه بنتيجة 2-1 ويحسم تأهله. وجاء الهدف المتأخر ليضع حداً لمواجهة قوية بين الفريقين، ويمنح النادي المغربي بطاقة العبور بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 3-2. ولحق المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه نهضة بركان، وصيف البطولة، الذي ضمن بدوره التأهل بعد إقصاء ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني، بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. ويعزز تأهل الفريقين الحضور المغربي في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، بعدما نجحا في تجاوز منافسيهما في الدور التمهيدي الثاني. الهلال السوداني يكرر فوزه على سيداما بونا وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الفريق فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليحجز مقعده في مرحلة المجموعات. وكان الهلال قد فاز بالنتيجة نفسها في مباراة الذهاب، ليحسم التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 4-0، مؤكداً تفوقه على منافسه في المواجهتين. وجاءت ثنائية الفريق السوداني في الشوط الأول، إذ افتتح إرنست لوزولو التسجيل في الدقيقة 33، قبل أن يضيف محمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» الهدف الثاني في الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط. ومنح الانتصار الهلال فرصة مواصلة مشواره القاري، كما عوض جماهيره جزئياً عن خروج غريمه التقليدي المريخ من المسابقة، بعدما ودع البطولة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وبهذا التأهل، يواصل الهلال تمثيل الكرة السودانية في البطولة، وسط تطلعات إلى تقديم أداء قوي في مرحلة المجموعات والمنافسة على بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية. سيمبا وكولوم يكملان قائمة المتأهلين وشهدت بقية مباريات الدور التمهيدي الثاني تأهل سيمبا التنزاني، بعدما حقق فوزاً عريضاً على فريق 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية بنتيجة 3-0. وجاء الانتصار ليمنح سيمبا تفوقاً كبيراً في مجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 9-1، بعدما كان قد حقق نتيجة إيجابية في لقاء الذهاب، ليعبر إلى المرحلة المقبلة بأفضلية واضحة. كما تأهل كولومب الكاميروني إلى مرحلة المجموعات، عقب فوزه على تينغيت السنغالي بهدف دون رد في مباراة الإياب، مستفيداً من انتصاره في لقاء الذهاب بنتيجة 2-0، ليحسم المواجهة بمجموع 3-0. وتعكس هذه النتائج اتساع رقعة المنافسة بين أندية القارة، مع نجاح فرق من تونس وموريتانيا والمغرب والسودان وتنزانيا والكاميرون في حجز مقاعدها بالمرحلة الرئيسية من البطولة. قرعة المجموعات الأربعاء المقبل تتجه أنظار الأندية المتأهلة إلى قرعة مرحلة المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، المقرر إجراؤها الأربعاء المقبل، حيث ستتحدد مواجهات المرحلة المقبلة ومسارات المنافسة نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. وتكتسب القرعة أهمية كبيرة بالنسبة إلى الفرق التي تجاوزت الدور التمهيدي، إذ ستتعرف من خلالها على منافسيها في مجموعاتها، في مرحلة تتطلب الاستعداد لمواجهات أكثر صعوبة أمام أندية تسعى بدورها إلى المنافسة على اللقب القاري. ومع اكتمال تأهل مجموعة من الأندية، تتطلع الفرق إلى استثمار نتائجها الإيجابية في الدور التمهيدي ومواصلة المشوار نحو الأدوار المتقدمة، بينما تبدأ الأندية المتأهلة الاستعداد لمرحلة جديدة من المنافسة على أحد أبرز ألقاب كرة القدم الأفريقية. football.summary: تأهل فريقا المغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد تحقيقهما انتصارات مهمة في مباريات الإياب. حيث تمكن المغرب الفاسي من الفوز على أسيك ميموزا العاجي بنتيجة 2-1 في أبيدجان، بعد أن تعادل الفريقان في مباراة الذهاب 1-1. سجل أهداف المغرب الفاسي كريستوفر إيبايي وخالد بابا، الذي أحرز هدف الفوز في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت بدل الضائع. من جهة أخرى، حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مريحاً على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليكرر نتيجة الذهاب. سجل إرنست لوزولو ومحمد عبد الرحمن "الغربال" أهداف الهلال في الشوط الأول. هذا التأهل يعوض الهلال خروج منافسه التقليدي المريخ من البطولة. كما تأهل سيمبا التنزاني وكولومب الكاميروني بعد انتصاراتهما في مبارياتهما.
